Difference-in-Differences in Stata — Day 2

What breaks when everyone adopts at a different time

KDIS Summer Workshop 2026

Day 2 of 2

How to use this document. This is a self-contained guide to Day 2: work through it on your own to review after class, or read ahead before it. Each step pairs the Stata command with the result it produces, so you can follow the reasoning on paper or open Stata and run along. To reproduce every figure and number here yourself, run programs/day2.do — it reproduces the entire day from the panel you built on Day 1.

1 Recap: the map from Day 1

How to review this section. Before starting anything new, rebuild Monday’s map from memory. Each question below is followed by its answer — so cover the answer, commit to your own first, and only then read on. Retrieving these ideas yourself is what makes the rest of the day land.

Here is Monday’s completed map again:

The DiD map

Question 1 — which single thing in this picture do we not observe? The dashed line. Every other element is data. The whole method is a rule for drawing that one line: take the control group’s change and apply it to the treated group’s starting point. The red bracket — the causal effect — is only as good as the dashed line.

Question 2 — state the assumption that lets us draw it. Had the program not existed, the treated group’s outcome would have changed by the same amount as the control group’s. The crucial part is that it is about trends, not levels: the 12-point gap between the lines is harmless and differenced out; only different trajectories are fatal.

Question 3 — Monday’s event study had flat pre-trends. Doesn’t that prove the assumption holds? No. It is worth sitting with why not before reading on; then look again at the break figure:

When it breaks

This world and the good one share every observed pre-period point; they differ only in the counterfactual, which no dataset contains. Flat pre-trends are supporting evidence, not proof. Keep that distinction warm. It is today’s load-bearing idea.

Question 4 — the mechanics. The 2×2 estimate is the interaction coefficient in reg y i.treated##i.post — the regression is the four-means arithmetic with a standard error attached — and we cluster at the level at which treatment was assigned: the district.

With the map fresh in your mind again, today’s question is simple to state: on Monday the map had a single red “program starts” line. Today every cohort has its own. What happens to the map — and who, exactly, is the control group?

2 Where we left off

On Monday we estimated the effect of the childcare program using one cohort — the districts that joined in 2007 — against districts that never joined. We got a clean event study, flat pre-trends, and an effect that grew from roughly zero to about 9.5 points over a decade.

But we threw away three quarters of the data. Today we use all of it.

table (adopt_year) if year == 2019, stat(freq)
-------------------
           |  Freq.
-----------+-------
adopt_year |
  2007     |     45
  2010     |     45
  2013     |     45
  2016     |     30
      .    |     15
-------------------

Four cohorts adopting in four different years, plus 15 districts that never adopt. This is what real policy rollouts look like. It is called staggered adoption, and it is the single most common structure in applied policy work.

twoway (connected emp_rate year if coh==0,    ...) ///
       (connected emp_rate year if coh==2007, ...) ///
       (connected emp_rate year if coh==2010, ...) ///
       (connected emp_rate year if coh==2013, ...) ///
       (connected emp_rate year if coh==2016, ...)
Cohort trends

3 The obvious generalization

Monday’s multi-period specification was:

\[ y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} \]

Nothing in that equation says the treated districts all had to start on the same date. \(D_{it}\) just switches from 0 to 1 whenever district \(i\) gets the program. So the natural thing to do — the thing essentially every paper did between 1994 and about 2018 — is run exactly the same regression on the full staggered panel.

gen byte treat = (year >= adopt_year) & !missing(adopt_year)
areg emp_rate treat i.year, absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
Linear regression, absorbing indicators             Number of obs     =  2,827
Absorbed variable: district_id                      No. of categories =    180
                          (Std. err. adjusted for 180 clusters in district_id)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
    emp_rate | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
       treat |   .1024949   .1858339     0.55   0.582    -.2642122     .469202
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 Read that coefficient

0.10 percentage points. Standard error 0.19. p = 0.58.

With 2,827 observations and 180 districts, we cannot distinguish the effect of this program from zero.

On Monday the same method on a quarter of the data gave 5.59 points, highly significant. Now, with four times as much data, the effect has vanished.

Something is wrong. The question is what.

4 Checking the assumption

The natural diagnosis is that parallel trends has failed. Adding the other cohorts brought in districts on different trajectories, and that contaminated the estimate. Let us check the way we learned on Monday: an event study.

One specification detail matters enormously here. Relative time now runs from −12 to +12, so we need the full set of lead and lag dummies. If you truncate the leads — say you only include lead_2 through lead_8 — every observation further out gets swept into the omitted reference category, and every coefficient in the regression is biased by it.

gen rel = year - adopt_year
forvalues k = 12(-1)2 { qui gen byte lead_`k' = (rel == -`k') & !missing(rel) }
forvalues k = 0/12    { qui gen byte lag_`k'  = (rel ==  `k') & !missing(rel) }

areg emp_rate lead_* lag_* i.year, absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
  PRE-PERIOD coefficients from the TWFE event study:
  ------------------------------------------------------
   k = -12   coef =   1.565   se = 0.326   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = -11   coef =   1.784   se = 0.304   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = -10   coef =   1.280   se = 0.270   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 9   coef =   1.177   se = 0.258   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 8   coef =   1.627   se = 0.229   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 7   coef =   0.836   se = 0.207   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 6   coef =   0.651   se = 0.224   p = 0.004   <-- significant
   k = - 5   coef =   1.032   se = 0.205   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 4   coef =   0.523   se = 0.147   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 3   coef =   0.543   se = 0.218   p = 0.013   <-- significant
   k = - 2   coef =   0.763   se = 0.195   p = 0.000   <-- significant
TWFE event study

A note on the figure. This one is titled with a question, not a finding. That is deliberate, and it is a habit worth copying: when I first built this plot I titled it “the pre-trend is an artifact”, which gave away the answer before anyone had looked at it. A figure should let the reader reach the conclusion. Compare it with the Day 1 conventions — reference period plotted as an explicit zero, vertical line at \(-0.5\) between the last pre- and first post-period, horizontal line at zero so the comparison is free.

Every single pre-period coefficient is statistically significant. Nine of the eleven have p-values below 0.001. Treated districts appear to have been on a systematically higher path for more than a decade before they adopted anything.

4.1 Before you read on

Write down your answer. This is the situation you will actually face.

You have a static estimate of essentially zero, and an event study whose pre-period is significant everywhere you look. What do you conclude, and what do you do next?

The natural answer is some version of: parallel trends fails here, the design is not credible, this dataset cannot answer the question. Many would shelve the project. That is the professionally responsible conclusion given the evidence in front of you.

It is also completely wrong.

5 The reveal

This data is simulated. We know the true effect of the program for every district in every year, because it was written into the data before any of it was estimated.

merge 1:1 district_id year using "${raw}/_dgp/true_effects.dta", ///
    keepusing(tau) keep(master match) nogen
replace tau = 0 if missing(tau)

sum tau if treat == 1
count if treat == 0 & tau != 0
  TRUE average treatment effect on the treated :  3.946
  Pre-period observations with a non-zero effect:    0
-------------------
           |   Mean
-----------+-------
adopt_year |
  2007     |  5.885
  2010     |  3.575
  2013     |  2.000
  2016     |  1.000
  Total    |  3.946
-------------------

Read those two numbers carefully.

The true effect is 3.95 percentage points. The program worked, and worked substantially. The static regression reported 0.10 — about 2.6% of the truth, and statistically indistinguishable from nothing.

Parallel trends holds exactly. Not approximately, not on average: there is not a single pre-period observation anywhere in the data with a non-zero treatment effect. The pre-trend you diagnosed does not exist.

5.1 What actually happened

Two things are true of this data, and both are true of most real policy rollouts:

  1. Effects grow over time. Childcare capacity takes years to build. A district five years in has a much larger effect than one in its first year.
  2. Cohorts differ. Districts that adopted early gained more per year than late adopters.

Neither is exotic. Neither violates parallel trends. But combined with staggered timing, they are enough to make the standard estimator return zero — and to make the standard diagnostic report a pre-trend that isn’t there.

The lesson. Your estimator was broken, and so was the test you used to check it. Both failures pointed at the same wrong conclusion.

6 Why it breaks: the Goodman-Bacon decomposition

Goodman-Bacon (2021) showed that the static two-way fixed effects estimate is a weighted average of all possible 2×2 comparisons in the data. Some of those comparisons are fine. Some should never be made.

bacondecomp requires a strongly balanced panel, and ours has holes, so we must drop any district with a gap first. Say so out loud when you report it:

bysort district_id: egen byte anymiss = max(missing(emp_rate))
keep if anymiss == 0
bacondecomp emp_rate treat, ddetail
graph export "${res}/day2_bacon_decomp.png", replace width(2000)
  Districts dropped to balance the panel: 46 of 180

Bacon Decomposition

|                      |         Beta   TotalWeight |
|----------------------+----------------------------|
|         Early_v_Late |  1.387045741   .0262094012 |
|         Late_v_Early |  -1.78121829   .0873646686 |
|         Early_v_Late |   2.89936924   .0524188024 |
|         Late_v_Early | -3.419722319   .1223105409 |
|         Early_v_Late |   1.26514709   .0594079744 |
|         Late_v_Early | -1.49956584   .0693093065 |
|         Early_v_Late |  4.188564777   .0555022624 |
|         Late_v_Early | -4.536407471   .0740030165 |

Note that dropping those 46 districts moves the static estimate slightly, from 0.102 on the full sample to 0.190 on the balanced one. So what we are decomposing here is not quite the headline regression. That is a real cost of the diagnostic, and it is the kind of thing you report rather than quietly absorb.

6.1 Reading the decomposition

Three kinds of comparison appear:

Type What it compares Legitimate?
Never_v_timing an adopting cohort against never-treated districts Yes
Early_v_Late early adopters against cohorts not yet treated Yes
Late_v_Early late adopters against cohorts already treated No

Look at the signs. Every Never_v_timing and Early_v_Late term is positive — between +0.88 and +4.19, bracketing the true effect. Every single Late_v_Early term is negative, from −0.94 down to −4.54.

And look at the weights. The forbidden Late_v_Early comparisons carry about 45% of the total weight. The clean never-treated comparison carries only 22%. Nearly half the estimate is built from comparisons that should not be made, and they push in the opposite direction. They very nearly cancel the real effect.

The graph bacondecomp draws makes the same point in one look — every 2×2 plotted against its weight:

Goodman-Bacon decomposition

Everything above the dashed line is a legitimate comparison. Everything below is a comparison that uses already-treated districts as controls — wrong sign, and several of the heaviest weights in the picture. The dashed line is their weighted average: 0.19, next to nothing.

6.2 Why “already treated” controls are poison

When a district that adopted in 2013 is compared against one that adopted in 2007, the 2007 district is used as the control. But by 2013 that district already has six years of program effect and is still improving. Its outcome is rising because of the treatment.

Subtracting a rising treated trend from another rising treated trend removes exactly the thing you are trying to measure. With effects that grow, the “control” outgrows the “treated”, and the comparison comes out negative.

This is also why the pre-period looked contaminated. Those forbidden comparisons do not politely confine themselves to the post-period.

7 Rebuilding the estimator by hand

The fix follows directly from the diagnosis: never use an already-treated district as a control.

For each cohort \(g\) and each period \(t\), compare the change in outcome from the year before adoption to \(t\), for cohort \(g\), against the same change for never-treated districts:

\[ \widehat{ATT}(g,t) \;=\; \underbrace{\big(\bar y_{g,t} - \bar y_{g,g-1}\big)}_{\text{cohort } g\text{'s change}} \;-\; \underbrace{\big(\bar y_{\text{never},t} - \bar y_{\text{never},g-1}\big)}_{\text{never-treated change}} \]

That is Monday’s 2×2, applied one cohort at a time. No new econometrics — just the discipline to keep the control group clean.

foreach g of local cohorts {
    forvalues t = `g'/`tmax' {
        local base = `g' - 1
        qui sum emp_rate if adopt_year == `g' & year == `t'      // a1
        qui sum emp_rate if adopt_year == `g' & year == `base'   // a0
        qui sum emp_rate if missing(adopt_year) & year == `t'    // c1
        qui sum emp_rate if missing(adopt_year) & year == `base' // c0
        post `M' (`g') (`t') ((`a1'-`a0')-(`c1'-`c0')) ...
    }
}
  Hand-built overall ATT =  3.864   (truth:  3.946)

  By cohort:
  +---------------------------+
  |    g   att_hat   att_true |
  |---------------------------|
  | 2007     5.370      5.904 |
  | 2010     4.283      3.563 |
  | 2013     1.783      2.006 |
  | 2016     0.506      0.998 |
  +---------------------------+

3.86 against a true 3.95. Four sample means per cell, no package, and it recovers what the standard method missed by a factor of forty.

The cohort pattern is right too: the 2007 cohort has the largest effect, and each later cohort has a smaller one — exactly the heterogeneity that broke TWFE. The 2016 estimate (0.51 vs a true 1.00) is the noisiest, which is what you should expect from 30 districts with only four post-adoption years.

8 Doing it properly: csdid

The hand-built version gets the point estimate right but has no valid standard errors, no covariates, and no principled aggregation. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) formalize exactly this estimator; csdid implements it.

gen gvar = cond(missing(adopt_year), 0, adopt_year)
csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) gvar(gvar) notyet
estat simple
Average Treatment Effect on Treated
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             | Coefficient  Std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         ATT |   3.951182   .2079284    19.00   0.000      3.54365    4.358715
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  >>> TRUE ATT =  3.946

3.951 against a true 3.946. The confidence interval [3.54, 4.36] comfortably contains the truth.

The gvar() option holds the cohort — the year each unit was first treated, with 0 for never-treated. notyet allows not-yet-treated units to serve as controls alongside the never-treated group, which buys precision. What it will never do is use an already-treated unit as a control.

csdid event study

Pre_avg is −0.003 with a p-value of 0.92. The pre-trend that was significant at every single lead has disappeared completely, on identical data. Nothing about the districts changed; only the comparisons we allowed the estimator to make.

The post-period recovers the true dynamic path: near 0.76 in the adoption year, rising steadily, flattening around 9.5 after a decade.

8.2 An honest caveat

Three individual pre-period coefficients — Tm8, Tm7, Tm1 — are still significant at the 5% level. That is not a failure of the estimator. It is what happens when you run eight hypothesis tests with only 15 never-treated districts: some come back significant by chance.

This is the point Roth (2022) makes formally. Individual pre-period coefficients are a noisy, low-powered basis for deciding whether a design is credible, in both directions. Passing the test does not certify parallel trends, and failing one lead does not condemn it. The Pre_avg of −0.003 is the more informative summary here.

9 The three estimators side by side

  +-------------------------------------+
  |                 est       b      se |
  |-------------------------------------|
  |         Static TWFE   0.102   0.186 |
  | Hand-built ATT(g,t)   3.864       . |
  |               csdid   3.951   0.208 |
  +-------------------------------------+
Comparison

One dataset. One question. Three answers, two of which are right.

On this figure. A coefficient plot like this is almost always a better way to compare estimators than a table, because the reader sees immediately where each estimate stands. The red dashed line at zero is the reference that matters: the static TWFE interval straddles it — “no effect” — while the two corrected estimators sit far from it, near the true 3.946. Note also yscale(reverse): without it, Stata puts the first estimator at the bottom, which reads backwards against the order you introduced them in.

10 Regenerating the table

On Monday we built Table 1 in code, and the stated reason was that you would have to rebuild it many times. Today is the demonstration.

Every number in Monday’s table is now wrong. Not slightly wrong — the headline estimate moved from 0.10 to 3.95, the standard errors changed, the sample changed, and the estimator changed. If that table had been typed into Word, you would now be retyping all of it, and hoping you caught every cell.

Instead:

eststo clear

eststo d1: qui areg emp_rate treat i.year, absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
estadd local est "Static TWFE"
estadd local ctl "All other districts"

qui csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) gvar(gvar) notyet agg(simple)
eststo d2
estadd local est "Callaway-Sant'Anna"
estadd local ctl "Not-yet-treated"

qui csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) gvar(gvar) agg(simple)
eststo d3
estadd local est "Callaway-Sant'Anna"
estadd local ctl "Never-treated only"

10.1 The one thing that will trip you up

csdid does not store its results for esttab the way areg does. If you run csdid and then estat simple, and then try to table it, you get:

. estat simple
Average Treatment Effect on Treated
         ATT |   3.951182   .2079284    19.00   0.000      3.54365    4.358715

. esttab .
estimates __000002 not found
r(111);

This is the failure that sends people looking for workarounds — extracting results by hand, or reaching for parmest to pull the coefficients into a dataset and rebuild the table manually. You don’t need to.

The fix is the agg(simple) option. It makes the aggregate ATT the posted estimation result rather than something you retrieve afterwards, so eststo and esttab behave exactly as they do after any other command:

csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) gvar(gvar) notyet agg(simple)
eststo d2   // just works

The coefficient is named ATT rather than treat, so — exactly as on Monday — rename() puts them on a single row.

local topts ///
    rename(treat DiD ATT DiD) keep(DiD) ///
    b(%9.3f) se(%9.3f) star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    coeflabels(DiD "Childcare program") varwidth(22) nodepvars nomtitles ///
    stats(est ctl N, fmt(%s %s %9.0g) ///
      labels("Estimator" "Comparison group" "Observations")) ///
    addnote("Outcome: maternal employment rate (pp)." ///
            "True ATT in this simulated data = 3.946 pp.")

esttab d1 d2 d3, `topts'
esttab d1 d2 d3 using "${res}/table2_staggered.rtf", replace `topts'
esttab d1 d2 d3 using "${res}/table2_staggered.tex", replace booktabs `topts'
----------------------------------------------------------------------
                                (1)             (2)             (3)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Childcare program             0.102           3.951***        4.010***
                            (0.186)         (0.208)         (0.241)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Estimator               Static TWFE    Callaway-Sant'Anna    Callaway-Sant'Anna
Comparison group       All other districts   Not-yet-treated   Never-treated only
Observations                   2827            2782            2782
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Standard errors in parentheses
Outcome: maternal employment rate (pp).
True ATT in this simulated data = 3.946 pp.
* p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01

Notice what column 3 buys you. Restricting to never-treated controls gives 4.010 with a standard error of 0.241; allowing not-yet-treated controls gives 3.951 with 0.208. Both bracket the truth. The notyet option bought precision without costing accuracy — and showing both columns is how you demonstrate that your result does not depend on the choice.

10.2 The master do-file

The argument for building tables in code is incomplete unless “rebuild everything” is an actual command you can run. That is what master.do is:

global root "..."          // the ONLY absolute path in the entire project

do "${prog}/day1.do"
do "${prog}/day2.do"

It also checks your packages before it starts, rather than failing halfway through:

foreach pkg in csdid drdid bacondecomp estout {
    cap which `pkg'
    if _rc {
        di as error "MISSING PACKAGE: `pkg'"
        exit 111
    }
}

Now do master.do rebuilds the data, both days of analysis, seven figures and two tables, in both Word and LaTeX, from nothing. When the referee report arrives, that is the difference between an afternoon and ten minutes.

A project that can only be reproduced by remembering which files to run in which order is a project you will eventually break — usually about eighteen months later, when you have forgotten, and the referee wants one more column.

11 What changed, and when

If you remember one section from today, make it this one.

Card and Krueger (1994) did not need any of today’s material. They had one treated state, one control state, one date. The 2×2 you built on Monday was a complete and correct tool for that problem.

What changed is not the econometrics of the 2×2 — that was always right. What changed is that researchers started applying it to settings it was never derived for: dozens of units adopting on dozens of dates, effects that evolve, cohorts that differ. Between roughly 1994 and 2018 the profession ran areg y treat i.year, absorb(id) on those settings and read the coefficient as an average treatment effect. Goodman-Bacon showed it usually isn’t one.

The modern literature is not a replacement for difference-in-differences. It is the same idea, defended against the ways a naive implementation goes wrong:

Problem Where it bites Tool
Already-treated units used as controls staggered adoption csdid, did_imputation, did2s
Contaminated event-study leads staggered adoption eventstudyinteract (Sun & Abraham)
Diagnosing where the weights went any staggered design bacondecomp
Pre-trend tests are underpowered everywhere Roth (2022)
“What if parallel trends is only nearly true?” everywhere honestdid (Rambachan & Roth)
Treatment turns on and off, or changes by steps non-absorbing / non-binary did_multiplegt_dyn (de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille)
Treatment is a dose, not on/off continuous treatments Callaway, Goodman-Bacon & Sant’Anna

11.1 The rule

If your units adopt treatment at different times, do not report a static two-way fixed effects coefficient as your headline estimate. Use an estimator that respects who is a valid control. If your units all adopt at the same time, Monday’s method is still correct and you do not need any of this.

12 Exercises

  1. Confirm the diagnosis. Re-run the static TWFE regression using only the 2007 cohort and the never-treated districts. Compare it to the 5.59 from Monday and to the 0.10 from the full panel. Which comparisons did dropping the other cohorts remove?

  2. Never-treated only. Re-run csdid without the notyet option, so only never-treated districts serve as controls. Compare the point estimate and the standard error. What did notyet buy, and what did it cost?

  3. Report it. Produce a single table with all three estimates, and write the two-sentence caveat you would put under it in a policy brief for a ministry that has not read Goodman-Bacon.

  4. Break it, then fix it. Try to build the Day 2 table using estat simple followed by esttab ., without agg(simple). Confirm you get the r(111) error. Then fix it. You will hit this in your own work and it is worth having seen the error message once, deliberately, rather than at midnight.

  5. Run the whole thing (optional). Delete everything in output/, then run master.do. Everything should come back identical. If it doesn’t, something in your project depends on state you didn’t record — find it.

    (One expected exception: .rtf files embed the time they were written, so they will not be byte-identical even though every number in them is. The .tex files and the figures should match exactly. Knowing which differences are real and which are metadata is part of the skill.)

Done in class, at the end of the day, in groups. Each group finishes exercises 1, 2, 3, and 4 before leaving (exercise 5 is an optional take-home — it needs rebuild time — and is not collected). Same format as Day 1: one do-file that runs top to bottom (day2_hw_group3.do) plus the log it writes, a display line naming the group members, and written answers as comments.

Completing the workshop — attending both days and submitting your group’s work each day — earns an Open Badge (Digital Badge), a verifiable and portable digital credential. The workshop carries no academic credit, and you will receive guidance on claiming your badge after the program.

13 Where to read next

  • Goodman-Bacon (2021), Journal of Econometrics — the decomposition you ran today.
  • Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021), Journal of Econometrics — the estimator behind csdid.
  • Sun & Abraham (2021), Journal of Econometrics — why event-study leads are contaminated.
  • Roth (2022), AER: Insights — why pre-trend testing misleads. Read this one first.
  • Rambachan & Roth (2023), Review of Economic Studies — sensitivity analysis instead of pre-testing.
  • de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020), American Economic Review — two-way fixed effects with heterogeneous effects, from a different angle than Goodman-Bacon.
  • de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2024), Review of Economics and Statistics — the dynamic estimator behind their did_multiplegt_dyn command. It handles the messy cases the others cannot: treatments that switch off again, and treatments that are not binary — a dose that steps 1 → 2 → 3, up or down. csdid allows neither.
  • Callaway, Goodman-Bacon & Sant’Anna, American Economic Review (forthcoming) — DiD when treatment is a dose (a subsidy rate, hours of service) rather than an on/off switch.
  • Roth, Sant’Anna, Bilinski & Poe (2023), Journal of Econometrics — the survey. Use its decision flowchart when you start your own project.
